course.title: Support & Resistance
course.summary: Learn to identify defensible support and resistance areas, interpret price behaviour around them, and form conditional scenarios without treating any zone as a guarantee.
course.description: An 18-lesson TradeThesis course on chart structure, support and resistance zones, price reactions, breakouts, invalidation and decision review. Imported as a working draft for editing and review.
course.catalogueHook: Read the evidence around a zone before deciding what it might mean.
course.problemStatement: Many traders draw levels as if they were exact barriers or automatic signals. This course teaches a more disciplined way to describe structure, evaluate zones and reconsider an interpretation when the evidence changes.
course.learningFocus: Observation → interpretation → conditional scenario → invalidation or reconsideration.

lessons.title: What support and resistance actually tell you
lessons.summary: Understand support/resistance as areas where responses may occur, not promises.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Understand support/resistance as areas where responses may occur, not promises.

The text below is the proposed wording shown to the learner. Instructor cues and production instructions are marked separately so they are not accidentally displayed as lesson copy.

### Welcome and set the task

**On screen:** 

> What support and resistance actually tell you

**On screen:** 

> Before we draw lines on a chart, let's learn what we are looking for.
>
> You do not need to know the answer yet. First, observe where price has been moving and what happened when it returned to certain areas.

### Chart A, unlabelled observation

**Show:** Chart A in its plain state. It should contain two or three visible occasions where declining price slows, pauses or turns upward in roughly the same broad area. No zone, line, arrows or explanatory labels appear yet.

**On screen:** 

> Look at the chart. Without trying to predict the next move, what stands out about the places where price pauses, turns or moves away?

**Response options:**
- Price reacted around a similar area more than once.
- Price is moving mostly in one direction.
- I see no clear pattern yet.
- I'm not sure.

**After response — on-screen feedback:**

> Good chart reading starts with describing what is visible. More than one interpretation may be reasonable at this stage. We are looking for evidence, not trying to guess the future.

### Name the idea: support

**Reveal:** Add a soft, horizontal band over the broad area containing the prior lower reactions. Avoid a hairline that implies an exact, uniquely correct price. Label the area **“prior reaction area”** first; then reveal the term **“support area.”**

**On screen:** 

> **Support** is an area where falling price has previously slowed, paused or turned upward.
>
> We use the word to describe what price did around that area in the history shown on the chart. It does not mean price must stop there the next time.

**Optional hover/expand note (not required to pass):**

> You will learn how to choose the boundaries of a zone later. For now, notice that the reactions occupy an area, not one perfectly exact price.

This preview is intentionally brief. The full “zones, not perfect lines” treatment remains Lesson 4.

### Chart B: resistance as the counterpart

**Show:** A second, equally clean illustration. Price rises into a broad area, pauses or turns downward on more than one occasion. Initially, show it without annotations.

**On screen:** 

> Now look at a similar situation from the other direction. What happened when price rose into this area?

**Response options:**
- It paused or turned down around a similar area.
- It moved through without a clear pause.
- I can't tell from this excerpt.

**Reveal:** Add a broad band around the prior upper reactions. Reveal the label **“resistance area.”**

**On screen:** 

> **Resistance** is an area where rising price has previously slowed, paused or turned downward.
>
> Support and resistance describe prior price behaviour. They are not a promise about the next move.

### The important counterexample: a zone can be crossed

**On screen:** 

> Based only on the earlier candles, we marked an area where price had reacted. What do you think we should expect the marking to guarantee?

**Options:**
- It guarantees price will turn there again.
- It marks an area worth watching, but the next move is uncertain.
- It guarantees that a trade should be taken there.

After the learner answers, reveal the additional candles crossing the band.

**On screen:** 

> Price has now moved through the area. That does not erase the earlier reactions; it shows that the area did not contain this move.
>
> A support or resistance area is a way to organise what we observe. It is not an unbreakable floor or ceiling, and it does not tell us by itself when to enter a trade.

### Observation versus explanation

**On screen:** 

> What can the chart tell us — and what can it not tell us?

**On-screen two-column reveal:**

**Visible observation**
- Price turned upward near this area on two earlier occasions.
- Price later crossed the same area.

**Possible interpretation, not proven by the chart alone**
- “Large institutions must be buying here.”
- “The zone will hold next time.”
- “A trade here is certain to work.”

**Student-facing copy:**

> A chart shows us price behaviour. It does not show the full reason for every move or the intentions of every participant.
>
> Good analysis begins with evidence. We can form a scenario, but we must leave room for price to behave differently.

### Short practice

**Show:** Two small, previously unseen illustrative chart excerpts labelled **A** and **B**. Chart A includes multiple pauses/turns in a broad area. Chart B includes a single close pass by a price level with no clear repeated reaction.

**On-screen question:**

> Which chart gives you clearer visible evidence of a prior reaction area? Choose one, then explain what you observed.

**Expected answer:** Chart A, because it shows more than one visible reaction around a similar area. The answer must not claim that the area is guaranteed to hold or that the chart proves who caused the reaction.

**Feedback if A selected with a reason:**

> Yes. You referred to what the chart shows: more than one reaction around a similar area. That makes it a reasonable area to pay attention to, not a guaranteed future turning point.

**Feedback if B selected:**

> Look again at how many times price visibly reacted around the area. A single pass may still be relevant in some contexts, but this exercise asks which excerpt shows clearer evidence of repeated prior reactions.

**Feedback if “I'm not sure”:**

> That is acceptable when the evidence is unclear. In chart reading, recognising uncertainty is better than inventing certainty. Compare the visible reactions and decide whether the evidence is strong enough to make a tentative observation.

### Knowledge check and takeaway

**On-screen takeaway:**

> **A zone is an area of interest, not a prediction.**

**On-screen knowledge check:**

**Q1. Which is the best description of support?**
- A guaranteed floor where price cannot fall further.
- An area where falling price previously slowed, paused or turned upward.
- A signal to buy whenever price touches it.

**Correct:** Second option.

**Q2. Price moves through an area that had previously acted as support. What can we conclude from this chart alone?**
- The original marking was necessarily useless.
- The market was manipulated by institutions.
- The area did not contain this move; the earlier reactions still occurred, and the new evidence matters.

**Correct:** Third option.

**Q3. Which statement is an observation rather than an unsupported explanation?**
- “Price turned upward near this area twice.”
- “Institutions bought here to defend the level.”
- “Price must reverse here again.”

**Correct:** First option.

**Completion behaviour:** Show brief feedback after each answer. Do not use high-stakes scoring or block course navigation for this introductory check. Require the learner to review a missed answer before marking the lesson complete, but allow retry.

lessons.title: Read structure before drawing
lessons.summary: Describe rising, falling, ranging, transitional or unclear structure before adding zones.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Describe rising, falling, ranging, transitional or unclear structure before adding zones.

### Set the task

**On screen:** 

> Read structure before drawing

**On screen:** 

> Before we mark support and resistance, let's first describe the path price has taken.
>
> Is it generally advancing, declining, moving sideways, or changing between those behaviours? You do not need to predict the next move. Start with what is already visible.

### Chart A: rising structure

**Show:** A clean, schematic sequence with an overall upward path. Several pullbacks form relative lows, and the price later rises to higher turning points. Include small fluctuations so the exercise does not look artificially perfect, but keep the broad structure legible.

**On screen:** 

> Which description best fits the overall path?

**Options:**
- Price is generally advancing.
- Price is generally declining.
- Price is moving sideways in a range.
- The structure is changing or unclear.
- I am not sure yet.

**After response — on-screen feedback:**

> Look at the larger turns, not each individual candle. The path is generally advancing: the later turning points are higher than the earlier ones. Small pauses and pullbacks do not automatically change that broader reading.

**Reveal:** Add three or four major turning-point markers one by one. Mark the sequence of relative lows and highs; do not draw a trendline or support zone.

**Voiceover / student-facing explanation:**

> A chart can move up without every candle rising. What matters here is the overall sequence of turns. In this example, the pullbacks find their way to higher areas, and price then advances to higher turning points. That supports a description of rising structure.

### Name the swing points

**Show:** Freeze the rising chart after the structure reveal. Point to one clear local peak and one clear local trough.

**On screen:** 

> A **swing high** is a relative turning point where price stopped rising and then moved lower in the surrounding sequence.
>
> A **swing low** is a relative turning point where price stopped falling and then moved higher in the surrounding sequence.
>
> They are identified from the relationship with nearby price action—not from one special candle shape.

**Reveal:** First highlight the swing high, then the swing low. Do not label every tiny fluctuation.

**On screen:** 

> Which point is the swing low?

Show three candidate markers, only one of which is the clear relative low used in the teaching example. The other two should be minor candle-to-candle fluctuations.

**Correct feedback:**

> Correct. This point stands out because price moved lower into it and then advanced away. We will learn to judge which turning points matter most in the next lesson.

**Incorrect feedback:**

> Look at the nearby sequence. A swing point is a relative turn in the surrounding movement, not simply any candle that is lower than the candle beside it.

### Chart B: falling structure

**Show:** A similarly styled schematic chart with an overall downward path. The highs and lows generally move lower, though some upward retracements occur.

**On screen:** 

> This chart contains some upward candles. What best describes its overall structure?

**Options:**
- Generally advancing.
- Generally declining.
- Moving sideways in a range.
- Changing or unclear.
- I am not sure yet.

**Reveal:** Mark a sequence of relative highs and lows, beginning with one high, then a lower high, then a lower low. Continue only as many marks as needed to show the structure.

**On screen:** 

> A declining structure can contain rallies. In this example, the rallies do not undo the broader sequence: later turning points are generally lower than earlier ones.
>
> Describe the sequence you can see. Do not assume that a declining structure must continue indefinitely.

### Chart C: a trading range

**Show:** A chart where price moves up and down within a broad, reasonably recognisable upper and lower area. Do not draw the boundaries in the initial state. The turns should not line up perfectly, because the course will later teach that chart areas are approximate.

**On screen:** 

> This chart has both rising and falling sequences. Which description fits the overall behaviour best?

**Options:**
- A clear rising trend.
- A clear falling trend.
- Price is moving back and forth within a broad range.
- The structure is too unclear to describe.

**Reveal:** Add several swing markers, then show a subtle top and bottom bracket spanning the broad trading area. Label only after the learner has answered: **“Trading range.”**

**On screen:** 

> A **trading range** is a period in which price moves back and forth within a broad area rather than making clear, sustained progress in one direction.
>
> The upper and lower boundaries need not be perfectly horizontal, and every high or low need not match the last one exactly. We are describing the overall structure, not measuring a perfect rectangle.

### Chart D: a trend-to-range transition

**On screen:** 

> At what point does the earlier rising behaviour become less clear? Select the first area where you would start questioning the original description.

Allow the learner to tap a candle or choose “I am not sure yet.”

**Reveal — state 2:** Extend the chart to show more overlapping movement within a developing range. Then mark a vertical divider labelled **“Earlier: rising structure”** and **“Later: less directional / possible range.”**

**On screen:** 

> Charts do not always switch from one neat category to another in a single candle.
>
> A move that was clearly advancing can start to lose direction. At first, the new structure may be uncertain. As more price action appears, a range may become easier to recognise.
>
> It is acceptable to say, “The structure is becoming less clear.” You do not need to force an immediate label.

### Independent practice: label the structure

**Show:** An unseen mixed chart in a neutral state. It should contain a clear sequence and 3–5 major turns, plus several minor candle fluctuations. This is not a zone-drawing task.

**On screen:** 

> Your turn.
>
> 1. Mark three to five turning points that help explain the overall path.
> 2. Choose the best description of the chart.
> 3. Write one sentence explaining the evidence you used.

**Classification options:**
- Generally rising.
- Generally falling.
- Broad trading range.
- Transition / unclear at this point.

**Reference-answer policy:** The reference overlay should identify a plausible set of major turns, not every possible minor turn. If the chart permits more than one reasonable reading, include a note explaining what evidence favours the reference description and what remains ambiguous.

**Expected reasoning:** The learner points to a sequence of relative highs/lows, repeated boundaries or loss of directional progress. “It looks bullish” or “there are many green candles” is not sufficient on its own.

**Feedback if sound:**

> Your description is tied to the path of price, which is the point of this exercise. Different traders may mark a nearby turn slightly differently; what matters here is whether your reading is supported by the visible sequence.

**Feedback if too many points are marked:**

> You have identified several local turns. Now step back and select the ones that best explain the larger path. We will work on deciding which turns matter most in Lesson 3.

**Feedback if the learner forces a trend label on an ambiguous chart:**

> Recheck the later part of the chart. Is price still making clear progress in one direction, or has the sequence become mixed? “Transition / unclear” is a valid answer when the evidence is mixed.

### Knowledge check

**Q1. What is a swing low?**
- Any candle with a lower low than the one before it.
- A relative turning point where price fell into an area and then moved higher in the surrounding sequence. **Correct.**
- A guaranteed support zone.

**Feedback:** A swing is a relative turn, not automatically a support zone and not every tiny fluctuation.

**Q2. Which description best fits a trading range?**
- Price moves back and forth within a broad area rather than making clear sustained progress in one direction. **Correct.**
- Every candle has to be the same size.
- Price cannot break out of its boundaries.

**Feedback:** A range describes the displayed behaviour. It is not a permanent container.

**Q3. What should you do when the structure becomes mixed?**
- Force a rising or falling label.
- Add support/resistance zones immediately.
- Describe the uncertainty and wait for more evidence if needed. **Correct.**

**Feedback:** Recognising uncertainty is part of good chart reading.

**Completion rule:** Show corrective feedback and allow retries. Do not require a perfect first attempt. The key objective is accurate structure vocabulary and observable reasoning.

### Close and handoff

**On screen:** 

> **Read the path of price before deciding where to draw.**

**On screen:** 

> You have learned to recognise relative turning points and describe the broader structure. Next, we will decide which of those turning points deserve attention—and which can be left alone.

**Do not preview zones in detail yet.** A short transition sentence is enough.

lessons.title: Identify meaningful swing points
lessons.summary: Select consequential swings without marking every local turn.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Select consequential swings without marking every local turn.

### Introduce the selection problem

**On screen:** 

> Identify meaningful swing points

**On screen:** 

> A chart may contain dozens of small turns. If we mark every one, the larger story becomes harder to see.
>
> This lesson is about choosing the turns that best explain the structure—not about finding a perfect answer that every trader must copy.

### The over-marked chart

**Show:** A controlled schematic chart containing 8–10 candidate turning points, including several meaningful turns and several small fluctuations. Initially do not label them or put dots on each one.

**On screen:** 

> Imagine you have 30 seconds to explain this chart to another trader. Which three or four turning points would you keep?
>
> You do not need to draw them yet. Choose the points that help you explain the larger path.

**Interaction:** Let the student tap up to four points. Also provide “I would keep more than four because…” as a short written justification, and “I am not sure yet.” The four-point constraint is for this learning exercise, not a universal trading rule.

**After response — feedback:**

> You have started to separate the larger structure from the smaller fluctuations. Now let's make the reasoning explicit.

### Teach the three filters

**On screen — filter 1: Relative prominence**

> **Does the turn stand out?**
>
> A small pause within a larger move may be less useful than a turn that marks a clearer change in the path. Look at the movement before and after the point, not just the candle itself.

**Reveal:** Highlight one major peak/trough and one minor fluctuation. Keep the markers neutral; do not display “good/bad” badges.

> Prominence is relative. We are not looking for the biggest candle or the sharpest wick by itself. We are asking whether the turn helps explain the sequence around it.

**On screen — filter 2: Structural role**

> **Does the turn help explain the structure?**
>
> A point may define a major reversal, help describe a rising or falling sequence, or sit near an edge of a broad trading range. A small turn that does not change our reading may be less important for this task.

**Reveal:** Highlight a point that helps describe the broader path and a minor inside fluctuation that changes little about the overall reading.

**On screen — filter 3: Relevance**

> **Does it help answer the question in front of you?**
>
> A point may be visible but not particularly helpful for the current analysis. Good chart reading includes deciding what not to mark.

### Correct two tempting shortcuts

**On screen:** 

> Two shortcuts that can mislead you

**Reveal one at a time:**

**Shortcut A:** “Keep the biggest candle.”

**Feedback copy:**

> A large candle can be part of an important move, but candle size alone does not tell you which turning point best describes the structure. Look at the surrounding sequence.

**Shortcut B:** “Keep the most recent turn.”

**Feedback copy:**

> A recent turn may matter, but recency alone does not make it structurally important. Compare it with the broader path and the question you are trying to answer.

### Reveal a reasoned selection

**Show:** Return to the over-marked chart. Reveal the intended reference points sequentially. After each point is highlighted, show a one-sentence rationale.

**Rationale templates for the asset writer:**
- “This turn helps describe the larger move because price moved clearly away and the subsequent sequence develops from it.”
- “This point helps define the broad range in this example.”
- “This smaller fluctuation is left unmarked because it does not materially change our description of the surrounding structure.”

**Important production constraint:** These are rationale templates, not pre-approved answers to assign blindly. The asset designer must write the final rationale to fit the final chart geometry. Every highlighted or omitted point must make visual sense once the chart is actually drawn.

**On screen:** 

> The reference version keeps the points that best explain this chart's structure. Other readings may be reasonable if they are supported by the visible movement.
>
> The goal is not to collect marks. It is to make the chart easier to understand.

### Independent practice: select and explain

**Show:** A separate unseen controlled chart with 8–10 possible local turns. Do not reuse the same pattern or place the important turns in exactly the same positions as the worked example.

**On screen:** 

> Choose up to four turns that best explain the overall structure.
>
> For each point, finish this sentence:
>
> “I kept this turn because it helps show __________.”
>
> Leave the other turns unmarked. You are allowed to say that one of the points is ambiguous.

**Interaction:** Tap-to-select candidate points, then select a rationale for each or enter a short sentence. Keep the interface light: the student should be reasoning about the chart, not completing a long form.

**Reference answer:** Three or four turns that show the chart's major path. The answer key should explain why each selected turn is useful and why at least two tempting candidates were omitted.

**Feedback if the learner selects many minor points:**

> Your selections include several local fluctuations. Step back and ask which turns change how you describe the larger path. Leave a point out when it adds little to that explanation.

**Feedback if the learner selects only one point:**

> One turn may be noticeable, but a single point often cannot explain the structure by itself. Look for a sequence that shows how price moved before and after it.

**Feedback if the learner's points differ but reasoning is defensible:**

> Your selections are not identical to the reference, but your explanation connects them to the visible structure. That is a defensible way to read a chart. Compare the reference to see what it prioritises differently.

**Feedback if points are selected only because price later moved:**

> Try not to use the later outcome as the only reason a point mattered. Explain what was structurally visible around the turn, without assuming the future move was obvious beforehand.

### Knowledge check

**Q1. Which is the most useful reason to retain a swing point?**
- It is the most recent point on the chart.
- It has the largest candle.
- It helps explain the broader price structure in the context of the question. **Correct.**

**Feedback:** Size and recency can be observations, but they are not sufficient on their own.

**Q2. If a chart has many visible local turns, what should you do?**
- Mark all of them equally.
- Select the points that best explain the structure and leave less useful turns unmarked. **Correct.**
- Keep only the turns followed by profitable trades.

**Feedback:** This is a structural reading exercise, not a hindsight contest.

**Q3. Can another trader mark a slightly different set of meaningful turns?**
- No, only one exact set is legitimate.
- Yes, if the alternative is supported by the chart and explained consistently. **Correct.**
- Yes, any random selection is equally useful.

**Feedback:** Reasonable interpretation is not the same as arbitrary interpretation. Evidence and explanation matter.

### Close and handoff

**On screen:** 

> **Choose the turns that explain the chart; leave the noise out.**

**On screen:** 

> You can now recognise structure and choose a smaller set of meaningful turns. Next, we will look at why the reactions associated with support and resistance are often better represented as areas than as perfect lines.

**Do not start teaching zone boundaries in the closing paragraph.** The next lesson should introduce that idea with its own chart and demonstration.

lessons.title: Zones, not perfect lines
lessons.summary: Use a band that accounts for related reactions instead of demanding one exact price.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Use a band that accounts for related reactions instead of demanding one exact price.

### Introduce the boundary problem

**On screen:** 

> Zones, not perfect lines

**On screen:** 

> Price often reacts around a similar area without turning at exactly the same price each time.
>
> If we insist on one perfect line, we may ignore part of what the chart shows. If we draw an area too wide, it may stop telling us anything useful. Let's examine that trade-off.

### Unlabelled chart: notice the variation

**Show:** Chart L04-A, a schematic price sequence with three related lower reactions. Their wick lows differ; bodies and closes cluster somewhat higher. Each reaction must be visually related to the same general area, but not identical. Price moves away from each area sufficiently for the learner to recognise the reactions.

**On screen:** 

> Look closely at the three reactions. Do they turn at exactly the same price?

**Options:**
- Yes, the low is identical each time.
- No, the lows vary, but the reactions are in a similar area.
- The chart does not show enough to compare.
- I am not sure yet.

**After response — feedback:**

> Notice the small differences between the reactions. The chart can show a related area without giving us one perfectly identical turning price.

### Name the practical representation

**Reveal:** Add a broad neutral bracket around the related reactions. Do not call it the final answer yet.

**On screen:** 

> A **zone** is an area used to describe related price reactions. Its boundaries help us organise the evidence; they are not a claim that every reaction must stop at the same tick.
>
> We want the area to include the behaviour we are trying to describe, without expanding so far that unrelated price movement becomes part of the same explanation.

**Voiceover:**

> There is judgement in this choice. The aim is not to make price fit a perfect line. The aim is to draw an area we can explain consistently from the chart.

### Wicks, bodies and closes

**Show:** Zoom to a single reaction candle, with wick and body visibly distinguishable. Then return to the cluster of reactions.

**On screen — reveal 1: Wicks**

> **Wicks** show the extremes price reached during the candle. They may help us see how far a reaction travelled, even if the candle did not finish near that extreme.

**On screen — reveal 2: Bodies and closes**

> **Bodies and closes** show where the candle opened and finished. They may help us judge where price spent more of the candle's visible range or where it ended the period.

**On screen — reveal 3: choosing a reference**

> Wicks, bodies and closes give us different information. Neither a wick-only nor a close-only boundary is the universal answer for every chart.
>
> Choose the reference that best explains the group of reactions you are examining, then apply that reasoning consistently.

### Compare three boundary choices

**Show:** The same L04-A chart in three sequential states. The underlying candles remain identical; only the proposed overlay changes.

**State A — too narrow:** A hairline or very thin band captures one wick extreme but excludes the other clearly related reactions.

**On screen:** 

> This boundary is so narrow that it leaves out much of the variation we are trying to describe. It may be precise on the screen, but it does not represent the group of reactions very well.

**State B — defensible reference zone:** A band spans the relevant cluster of lower reactions and related body/close area, while remaining clearly separated from unrelated movement.

**On screen:** 

> This is a defensible zone for this example. It captures the related reactions and leaves enough distinction for us to explain where the area sits.
>
> Another analyst may choose a slightly different boundary and still have a reasonable explanation.

**State C — too broad:** A large band captures the reaction cluster plus substantial unrelated movement above and below.

**On screen:** 

> This band is so wide that it covers much more than the reactions we are trying to describe. It becomes harder to explain what the zone actually represents.

**Production requirement:** Do not call State B “the objectively correct zone” or score it as a single exact numerical answer. Its purpose is to demonstrate a reasoned middle ground.

### Show that the same reasoning can apply at resistance

**Show:** A second short schematic chart containing several related upper reactions. Initially unlabelled; wick highs differ and the bodies/closes occur somewhat lower.

**On screen:** 

> The reactions are now near the upper part of the chart. What should remain consistent about the way you choose the area?

**Options:**
- The zone should capture the related reactions without becoming unnecessarily broad.
- The zone must touch every wick exactly and have no width.
- The zone should be as wide as possible so price cannot leave it.
- I am not sure yet.

**Reveal:** Show a defensible upper reaction band.

**On screen:** 

> The direction of the reactions changes; the reasoning does not. Look at the related price behaviour, choose boundaries you can explain, and avoid pretending the edge is perfectly exact.

### Independent practice: defend a zone

**On screen:** 

> Choose a zone around the related reactions.
>
> Then complete this sentence:
>
> **“I chose these boundaries because…”**
>
> You may use wicks, bodies/closes, or a combination. Your explanation matters more than matching the reference drawing exactly.

**Interaction:** Prefer a simple zone-width selection or chart tap/control that can be used on mobile. If an actual drawing interaction is not available during content review, use three candidate overlays of different widths and ask the student to select and explain. Do not force a fine drag gesture on a phone for this concept lesson.

**Reference key:** Identify a defendable zone, and explain what the upper and lower boundaries include. Add notes explaining why the narrow alternative misses relevant reactions and why the broad alternative absorbs unrelated movement.

**Feedback if the zone is too narrow:**

> Your zone captures one extreme, but consider whether it represents the other related reactions too. What evidence would be left outside your boundary?

**Feedback if the zone is too broad:**

> Your zone includes the reaction cluster, but also a large amount of unrelated movement. Try reducing its width while still accounting for the reactions you chose to describe.

**Feedback if the zone differs from the reference but is defensible:**

> Your boundaries differ slightly from the reference, but your explanation uses the visible candles consistently. That is a reasonable interpretation. Compare what each boundary includes and excludes.

**Feedback if the reason is “because that is where price will turn”:**

> We cannot know that a zone will hold next time. Explain the boundary from the reactions visible in the chart, rather than from a prediction about future price.

### Knowledge check

**Q1. Why might a zone be more useful than one thin line?**
- Related reactions may occur across a range of prices rather than at an identical point. **Correct.**
- A zone guarantees price cannot pass through it.
- A line is never useful in any circumstance.

**Feedback:** Some traders may use lines in particular contexts. This lesson teaches why a zone is a practical representation when related reactions vary.

**Q2. Which statement about wicks and bodies is most accurate?**
- Wicks always determine the only correct boundary.
- Candle bodies and closes must always determine the only correct boundary.
- Wicks, bodies and closes show different aspects of price movement; the chosen reference should fit the reactions being explained. **Correct.**

**Feedback:** Explain the information used and keep the method consistent.

**Q3. What is the main problem with a zone that is extremely wide?**
- It may include so much unrelated movement that it becomes less informative. **Correct.**
- It guarantees a loss.
- It ensures the zone will always hold.

**Feedback:** The band should explain a meaningful area; maximum width is not the goal.

### Close and handoff

**On screen:** 

> **A useful zone captures the relevant reactions without pretending the boundary is exact.**

lessons.title: Choose the right areas and reduce clutter
lessons.summary: Prioritise useful areas and remove low-value marks.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Prioritise useful areas and remove low-value marks.

### Make the new challenge feel meaningful

**On screen:** 

> Choose the areas that matter

**On screen:** 

> You can now recognise the structure of a chart and identify places where price has reacted before. The next challenge is deciding what deserves to stay on the chart.
>
> A useful chart does not show everything you noticed. It shows the areas that help you explain what matters.

### The cluttered chart

**Show:** A schematic chart with seven or eight candidate horizontal marks or bands. Include a mix of: a broad prior range edge, a major turning area, two nearby marks that may be redundant, a tiny local fluctuation and one mark far from the current chart question. Do not mark which ones are “good” or “bad.”

**On screen:** 

> Imagine you have to explain this chart to another trader. Which areas would you keep, combine or leave out?
>
> You are not being asked to find the one perfect answer. Choose the areas you can explain with evidence.

**Interaction:** Let the learner tap candidate marks to classify each as **Keep**, **Combine with another area**, **Leave out for this reading**, or **Not sure yet**. They should be able to revise a selection before submitting. Avoid dragging all lines around at this stage; the lesson is about selection, not precision drawing.

**After submission — neutral feedback:**

> Your choices give us something to examine. The important part is not how many marks you kept; it is whether each one adds useful information.

Do not grade the initial selection heavily. It is a diagnostic moment and should create a reason to learn the filters.

### Teach the selection filters

**Reveal the heading:**

> Three questions help you decide what stays

Reveal each one at a time, with one highlighted candidate mark on the chart.

**On screen — filter 1: Is it anchored in structure?**

> Does this area relate to a meaningful turn, a cluster of related reactions or an edge of the range? Or is it simply a small fluctuation that happens to be easy to mark?

**On screen — filter 2: Does it add information?**

> Does this area tell us something different from a nearby area we have already kept? If two marks describe the same broad region, do we need both?

**On screen — filter 3: Is it relevant to the chart question?**

> Does this area help explain the part of the chart we are studying now? An area can be real in the historical chart and still not be central to the current reading.

### Watch the chart become easier to read

**Show:** Return to the same cluttered chart. Remove one mark at a time. The learner must see exactly what changed and why; do not replace the entire image instantly with a “perfect” version.

**Reveal sequence:**

1. Remove a tiny local fluctuation that does not explain meaningful structure.
2. Combine two nearby marks that refer to the same broad reaction area.
3. Leave out an area that is distant from the current question, while noting it could be relevant in another analysis.
4. Keep a major area that is tied to clear structure.

**On screen:** 

> We removed this mark because it added little beyond the structure already shown.

> We combined these marks because the chart supports treating them as one broader area for this exercise.

> We left this area out of the current reading. That does not mean it can never matter; it simply is not helping answer today's question.

> We kept this area because it connects to a clear structural feature. It is still an area to observe, not a guarantee of future behaviour.

### Give the learner a practical constraint

**On screen:** 

> For the next exercise, try to keep no more than three or four primary areas. This is a practice constraint to help you focus—not a rule that every trading chart must contain four zones or fewer.

**Prompt:**

> Before you continue, complete this sentence: “I kept these areas because… I left out or combined these because…”

**Interaction:** Short text entry or selection plus a concise justification. Do not require lengthy prose on mobile.

**Feedback guidance:** Credit reference to structure, redundancy and relevance. Do not award extra credit for using the fewest possible zones if important context was omitted.

### Knowledge check

**Q1. Why should a chart not be filled with every possible zone?**

A. A chart is always limited to four zones in real trading.  
B. Too many marks can obscure the structure and add little information.  
C. A chart with fewer zones guarantees a better trade.

**Correct answer:** B.

**Feedback:**

> Exactly. The number is not the rule. The aim is to keep the areas that help explain the chart and leave out marks that add little to the current reading.

**Q2. If your zone differs from the reference drawing, what should you examine first?**

A. Whether your boundary is pixel-perfect.  
B. Whether your zone captures the relevant reactions and has a defensible width.  
C. Whether your zone guarantees the next price move.

**Correct answer:** B.

**Feedback:**

> Compare the evidence and the boundary logic. The reference is a reasoned example, not a promise that only one exact drawing can be valid.

### Close and give earned encouragement

**On screen:** 

> **A useful chart is selective. Keep the areas you can explain.**

**On screen:** 

> You have now moved from recognising a reaction to choosing which areas deserve attention—and made your first complete support-and-resistance drawing attempt.
>
> That is a real step forward. You are not expected to have a finished method yet. The next lesson is about making your boundaries more consistent and explaining exactly why you placed them where you did.

**Chart Reading Notes prompt:**

> I kept these areas because…  
> I left out or combined… because…  
> One part I still find uncertain is…

Keep the encouragement specific and proportionate. It should acknowledge the new skill, not imply proficiency from completing one exercise.

lessons.title: Set defensible zone boundaries
lessons.summary: Explain boundary choice with visible reactions, wicks and bodies.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Explain boundary choice with visible reactions, wicks and bodies.

### Connect selection to drawing

**On screen:** 

> Set boundaries you can explain

**On screen:** 

> Last lesson, you chose which areas deserved attention. Now we will work on the drawing itself.
>
> The question is not “What is the one perfect price?” It is “Which boundaries describe the reactions I am trying to capture, without making the zone meaningless?”

### Observe the variation first

**Show:** A schematic support example in which three lower reactions occur in the same broad region, but their wick extremes, candle bodies and closes are not identical.

**On screen:** 

> Look carefully at these reactions. Do they all turn at one identical price, or do they occupy a range?

**Response choices:**
- The reactions line up exactly.
- The reactions are near one another but vary.
- I cannot tell from this view.

**Reveal:** Highlight the related lows and show light guide marks for the wick extremes and body/close area. Do not draw the final zone yet.

**On-screen feedback:**

> The reactions are related, but they are not identical. A useful zone needs to represent that variation while still preserving a meaningful area.

### Establish the boundary method

**On-screen — heading:**

> A defensible zone starts with a reason

Reveal the four steps one at a time.

**Step 1 — Anchor the area.**

> Start with the meaningful swing or group of related reactions. Do not start by choosing a width that looks neat and then searching for candles to justify it.

**Step 2 — Inspect the candles involved.**

> Look at the relevant wick extremes and where the bodies and closes sit. Ask which parts of the candles help describe the reaction you are marking.

**Step 3 — Test whether the band captures the evidence.**

> Does the area include the related reactions you are trying to represent? Or does it miss an important part of the cluster?

**Step 4 — Test whether the band stays useful.**

> Is the zone so wide that it covers unrelated price action and stops helping you distinguish where the reaction occurred?

### Compare three choices

**Show in sequence, all on the same chart:**

1. A too-narrow line/band that captures only the very tips of one reaction and misses related variation.
2. A defensible zone that captures the relevant cluster.
3. An overly broad band that swallows candles and movement not needed to describe the reaction.

**On screen:** 

> What does this boundary include—and what important information might it miss or blur?

**Reveal 1 — too narrow:**

> This mark is precise on the screen, but it does not represent the full group of reactions we are examining. A thin line is not automatically more accurate simply because it looks exact.

**Reveal 2 — defensible:**

> This zone captures the main reaction area while keeping its boundaries tied to visible structure. Another trader might choose slightly different edges and still describe the same area reasonably.

**Reveal 3 — too broad:**

> This band covers so much unrelated price action that it becomes harder to explain what the zone actually represents. Wider is not automatically safer or better.

### A consistent convention matters more than copying a drawing

**Show:** Two side-by-side versions of the same reaction area. One convention is more wick-inclusive; the other gives greater emphasis to the body/close cluster while still acknowledging the excursion.

**On screen:** 

> A wick can show how far price briefly travelled. The body and close can show where the candle finished. Both can be useful observations, but neither gives a universal answer on its own.
>
> Choose a boundary convention that makes sense for the chart, explain why it captures the relevant reactions, and apply it consistently. Do not quietly change the rule from candle to candle just to make the old drawing look right.

**Prompt:**

> Which version would you use for this chart, and what evidence would you use to explain your choice?

**Feedback principle:** Accept either version if the written explanation fits the chart and the band remains useful. If a selected version excludes a defining reaction or covers an excessive amount of unrelated movement, ask the student to reconsider that evidence.

### Apply the same thinking at resistance

**Show:** A separate upper-reaction chart with varied wick highs and body/close placement. Begin unlabelled.

**On screen:** 

> Now apply the same reasoning from the other direction. Which upper reactions belong to the area, and what would make your zone too broad?

**Reveal:** Add a reference band after the student responds.

**On-screen explanation:**

> The direction has changed, but the reasoning has not. Start from the related structure, inspect the candle ranges and closes, and choose boundaries that capture the area without swallowing unrelated movement.

### Independent practice: defend your own boundaries

**Show:** A new, unlabelled schematic chart with one coherent lower reaction cluster. It should be somewhat less tidy than the first demonstration but still interpretable.

**On-screen instructions:**

> 1. Mark a support zone around the relevant reactions.
> 2. Before looking at the reference, complete the three short prompts below.

**Prompts:**
- What is the structural anchor for your zone?
- Which candle features or reactions determined your boundaries?
- What nearby movement did you choose not to include, and why?

**After submission — model comparison:** Reveal the reference band with two brief notes: “Why this area was captured” and “A reasonable alternative.” The alternative should be real, not token language; if no alternative is defensible on this chart, the note should say why.

### Knowledge check

**Q1. Which is the best reason to make a zone a little wider than one thin line?**

A. Wider zones are always safer.  
B. Related reactions occupy a range, and the chosen band should capture the relevant evidence without becoming vague.  
C. A broad zone makes a future reaction more likely.

**Correct answer:** B.

**Feedback:**

> The width should describe the reaction area. It is not a way to guarantee a future outcome.

**Q2. Two students draw slightly different zones around the same cluster. What should we examine?**

A. Which drawing matches the reference pixels exactly.  
B. Whether each drawing has a structural anchor, captures the relevant reactions and remains usefully bounded.  
C. Which student sounds more confident.

**Correct answer:** B.

**Feedback:**

> A reasonable alternative can still be defensible. The drawing must be supported by the chart, not by confidence or visual imitation.

### Close and give the learner a usable principle

**On-screen takeaway:**

> **A good boundary has a reason. Precision without evidence is only decoration.**

**On-screen closing copy:**

> You have now moved beyond spotting an area. You have practised explaining where it begins, where it ends and why those limits are useful.
>
> The next lesson is about the other half of clear chart work: knowing what to remove. Even a well-drawn zone may not deserve to stay on every chart.

**Chart Reading Notes prompt:**

> I chose these boundaries because…  
> A reasonable alternative could be…  
> I would reconsider my width if…

lessons.title: Keep the chart readable
lessons.summary: Remove marks that do not improve explanation.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Remove marks that do not improve explanation.

### Set the editing task

**On screen:** 

> A clear chart is edited, not just marked

**On screen:** 

> A zone can be drawn reasonably and still not help the current analysis.
>
> Today you will practise editing a chart. You are not trying to erase every detail; you are trying to keep the details that help explain the structure.

### Ask what the marks actually help explain

**Show:** A chart covered with about six or seven zones, including repeated overlapping marks, a minor local mark, a major structural area, and one meaningful but distant area.

**On-screen prompt:**

> Which of these marks helps you explain the part of the chart we are looking at now? Which marks repeat information or pull your attention away?

**Interaction:** Let the learner select zones as **Keep**, **Combine**, **Leave out for this reading**, or **Uncertain**. If the interface cannot support selections per band, use a short numbered list with a chart legend. Do not require precise drawing yet.

**On-screen response after attempt:**

> Before removing anything, decide what job each mark is doing. A mark should earn its place by helping answer a question about this chart.

### Demonstrate three reasons to edit

Reveal the reasons one at a time. Each reason should highlight the exact band involved.

**Reason 1 — It repeats information already present.**

> These two nearby bands describe the same broad reaction region for the question we are asking. Combining them makes the structure easier to read without losing a distinction this chart needs.

**Caution:** Combine only when the areas are genuinely redundant for the present analysis. If the two bands represent different structural pivots or different parts of a range, keep that distinction visible.

**Reason 2 — It is weakly anchored.**

> This mark sits near a small fluctuation but does not help explain the larger movement. We can acknowledge that price moved there without promoting every pause to a main zone.

**Caution:** “Minor” does not mean “never relevant.” A small area may matter to a different, more local question. We are choosing the focus for this chart, not declaring universal irrelevance.

**Reason 3 — It is not needed for the current question.**

> This area is part of the broader history, but it is far from the section we are studying. Leaving it out helps us concentrate on the current structure. We can bring it back if the question changes.

**Caution:** If the distant zone is needed to understand the visible chart's overall range, do not remove it just to produce a sparse image. The actual chart must make the decision defensible.

### Reveal the chart becoming clearer

**Show:** Remove or merge one mark per reveal. Keep the previous state available as a brief toggle or “see previous version” action.

For each edit, show:
- the band changed;
- whether it was removed or combined;
- the specific reason; and
- what information remains represented afterward.

**On-screen copy after the last edit:**

> Notice what changed: we did not discover a secret level. We made the chart's main structure easier to explain by removing marks that were not earning their space.

### Explain the exercise constraint

**On screen:** 

> For the next chart, aim to keep no more than four primary areas. This limit is a way to practise prioritising. It is not a universal rule for trading charts.

**Prompt:**

> For each area you keep, you should be able to finish the sentence: “This stays because…”

### Independent practice: edit another chart

**Show:** A new schematic chart with five or six candidate zones. Include one clear structural area, two overlapping/redundant marks, one minor fluctuation and one area that is potentially meaningful but not central to the question.

**On-screen instructions:**

> Edit the chart for this question: “Which areas best explain the main structure shown here?”
>
> Keep, combine or leave out each candidate area. Then write one short reason for one mark you kept and one you removed or combined.

**Response structure:**
- Area kept because…
- Area removed/combined because…
- One area I am unsure about is…

### Compare, don't copy

**Reveal:** The reasoned reference version, then highlight each key decision.

**On-screen copy:**

> Compare the jobs of the retained marks. Did you keep the important structure? Did any two of your zones repeat the same information? Did you remove something that you can now explain was useful?
>
> Your chart does not need to look identical to this one. If a different selection preserves the important structure and you can defend it, that is worth keeping.

### Knowledge check

**Q1. You remove a zone because it does not help answer the question in this chart. What does that mean?**

A. The area can never matter in future analysis.  
B. It is not needed for this particular reading; a different question may make it relevant.  
C. All distant zones should always be deleted.

**Correct answer:** B.

**Feedback:**

> Editing is contextual. You are choosing what helps this reading, not declaring that an area is permanently meaningless.

**Q2. When should two nearby zones be combined?**

A. Whenever they are close together on the screen.  
B. When they describe the same broad region for the current question and combining them does not hide a meaningful distinction.  
C. Always combine all nearby zones to reduce clutter.

**Correct answer:** B.

**Feedback:**

> The decision depends on what the areas represent, not just their visual distance.

### Close with the feeling of control

**On-screen takeaway:**

> **Every mark should have a job. Leaving something out is a decision too.**

**On-screen closing copy:**

> You can now do more than add zones. You can edit your analysis, explain what stays and deliberately leave out what does not help.
>
> Next, we will look at how to evaluate a zone's usefulness without pretending there is a magic number that tells us how strong it is.

**Chart Reading Notes prompt:**

> I removed or combined… because…  
> The most useful area I kept was… because…  
> If my chart question changed, I might reconsider…

lessons.title: Evaluate a zone without inventing a magic score
lessons.summary: Review zone relevance contextually, not with a universal numeric score.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Review zone relevance contextually, not with a universal numeric score.

### Reframe the question

**On screen:** 

> What makes a zone worth paying attention to?

**On screen:** 

> You can now choose areas, draw boundaries and remove marks that do not help your reading. The next question is more subtle: why is one area worth paying attention to at all?
>
> We will examine the evidence without turning it into a magic score or pretending a zone can guarantee what price will do.

### Compare two candidate zones

**Show:** Two schematic chart excerpts side by side, both with candidate areas highlighted in a neutral style but no labels saying which is better.

- **Area A:** several crossings/touches, some noisy, overlapping movement and no single clear structural anchor in the shown excerpt.
- **Area B:** fewer visible reactions but a clearer relationship to a turning point or broader range structure, with visible movement away from the area.

Do not make Area B unrealistically perfect, and do not make Area A obviously meaningless. Students should need to reason.

**On-screen prompt:**

> One area has more visible visits. The other has fewer, but its reactions are easier to describe. What would you inspect before deciding which area is more useful for this chart?

**Response options:**
- Count the touches and select the higher number.
- Examine structure, how the reactions behave, and whether the area helps explain the current chart.
- Choose whichever area price touched most recently.
- I would need more context before deciding.

**Feedback for the evidence-based choice:**

> Good. A count is an observation, but it does not explain what those visits mean. We need to look at how the area fits the structure and what the chart actually shows.

**Feedback for “need more context”:**

> That may be the most defensible response. You can describe evidence in the visible excerpt while remaining uncertain about how important the area is in a broader view.

### Build a qualitative review, one question at a time

**On-screen heading:**

> Five questions—not a score

Reveal each question as a short inspection prompt. Do not number them as points or let the user total them into a percentage.

**Question 1 — What anchors the zone?**

> Does it relate to a meaningful swing, a cluster of related reactions or an edge of a broader range? Be able to point to that structure.

**Question 2 — How clear are the reactions?**

> Are the reactions recognisably related, or are we grouping together price movements that do not really describe the same area?

**Question 3 — What happened after the reactions?**

> Did price visibly move away, pause, overlap or cross repeatedly? Describe the behaviour. Do not assume that a clear departure proves the same thing will happen again.

**Question 4 — Where is the area in the current chart?**

> Is it relevant to the part of the chart we are studying? Are there other areas nearby that change what this one helps us explain?

**Question 5 — What remains uncertain?**

> Could another reasonable reading exist? Is this only a local view? What information is not visible in the chart excerpt?

### Correct the three common shortcuts

Reveal each statement, ask the student to choose **Helpful**, **Not a reliable rule**, or **Needs context**, then show the explanation.

**Shortcut A:** “Three touches makes a level strong.”

**Reveal explanation:**

> Three touches is a count, not a complete explanation. Were the reactions clear? Did they describe the same area? What was price doing around them? The count alone cannot answer that.

**Shortcut B:** “Every additional touch makes the zone stronger.”
**Reveal explanation:**

> Additional visits add information about how price is interacting with the area, but they do not automatically improve or weaken it. The behaviour and broader context matter.

**Shortcut C:** “A zone becomes weak after every retest.”

**Reveal explanation:**

> That is also too simple. A retest is a new interaction to interpret, not a universal verdict. We will later study how evidence can change as price revisits, crosses or moves away from an area.

### Apply the review to one area

**Show:** A new area with a clear structural anchor but some ambiguity around the exact extent of related reactions.

**On-screen prompt:**

> Complete both sentences:
>
> “This area is worth watching in this chart because…”
>
> “What remains uncertain is…”

**Model response shown after attempt:**

> “The area relates to a prior turning point and two reactions in a similar region. The chart gives me a reason to mark it, but it does not tell me whether price will react the same way next time.”

### Knowledge check

**Q1. A candidate zone has five visible visits, but the reactions are noisy and its structural role is unclear. What can you conclude?**

A. Five visits make it the strongest zone on the chart.  
B. The area has been visited several times, but the count alone does not establish its usefulness.  
C. The zone must fail because it has been touched too often.

**Correct answer:** B.

**Feedback:**

> The count is one observation. Look at how the area fits the structure, how price behaved around it and what remains uncertain.

**Q2. In Uneven Lows, what matters most when comparing your support band with the reference?**

A. Every low must be inside a perfectly level line.  
B. Whether your band captures the related structure with defensible boundaries and a clear rationale.  
C. Whether you predicted the next price movement correctly.

**Correct answer:** B.

**Feedback:**

> The task is to represent the related reaction area, not to force all lows to match or predict the next move.

### Close the first three skills as one achievement

**On-screen takeaway:**

> **Evaluate the evidence. Do not turn it into a magic number.**

**On-screen closing copy:**

> Look at what you can now do that you could not do at the start of this course. You can recognise structure, select the areas that matter, draw boundaries you can explain, simplify the chart and question your own assumptions about a zone.
>
> You have not learned to predict every reaction—and that is not the goal. You have begun to build a repeatable way to read a chart and explain your decisions. The next module turns to what price does as it approaches and interacts with these areas.

**Chart Reading Notes prompt:**

> This zone is worth attention because…  
> The visible evidence is…  
> The part I cannot know from this chart alone is…

**Tone note:** This is the strongest progress acknowledgement in Lessons 5–8 because the learner has now connected selection, drawing, editing and evaluation. Keep it concrete and modest. No “you are now a professional trader” language, no return claims and no badge implying mastery.

lessons.title: Read the approach to a zone
lessons.summary: Describe approach behaviour before the zone is reached; separate observation from interpretation.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Describe approach behaviour before the zone is reached; separate observation from interpretation.

### Open on a practical question

**On screen:** 

> Read the approach to a zone

**On screen:** 

> A zone gives us an area to pay attention to. But price does not arrive there in the same way every time.
>
> Today, we will look at the journey toward an area—not just the area itself.

**Production note:** A small progress line may show “Lesson 9 of 18.” Do not add a triumphant animation. The learner should feel they are entering a more applied stage, not that they have already mastered the skill.

### Controlled Chart A: a more directional approach

**On screen:** 

> Before price reaches the area, describe the path it is taking. What do you notice about the candles and the recent swings?

**Response choices:**
- Price is advancing with relatively little overlap.
- Price is moving back and forth with substantial overlap.
- The excerpt is too short for me to tell.

Allow a short free-text response if the lesson platform supports it.

**After response — feedback:**

> You are describing the approach, not predicting the result. Keep those two jobs separate.

**Reveal sequence:**
1. Highlight the sequence of recent swing points.
2. Highlight the comparatively directional run toward the band.
3. Keep future candles hidden.

**Student-facing explanation:**

> Here, price has moved toward the area in a relatively directional way. That is an observation about the route it has taken so far.
>
> It does **not** tell us that the area must break. Price could continue, pause, turn away or produce mixed evidence. The approach gives us context; it does not give us certainty.

### Controlled Chart B: a hesitant, overlapping approach

**Chart B brief:** Use a second schematic chart approaching a comparably clear area. This time the path includes overlapping candles, short back-and-forth moves and less clean directional progress. Keep scale and visual styling similar to Chart A, so differences in the approach are visible without decoration.

**On screen:** 

> The destination is similar. What differs in the path price takes to get there?

**After the learner responds, reveal:**
- A subtle bracket over the overlapping sequence.
- The recent local swing points.
- The target zone, without showing the eventual reaction.

**Student-facing explanation:**

> This approach has more overlap and less consistent progress in one direction. That tells us something about the route, but not the result.
>
> Avoid turning descriptions into automatic rules. A directional approach does not guarantee a break, and an overlapping approach does not guarantee a rejection. We are building context, not a formula.

**Compare interaction:** Ask the learner to finish both statements:
- “On Chart A, I noticed …”
- “On Chart B, I noticed …”

**Model response:** Chart A advanced more directionally with fewer overlapping candles; Chart B moved back and forth more. Both remained uncertain as to what would happen at the zone.

**Acceptable alternatives:** Students may refer to the swing sequence or the degree of overlap, if these observations match the actual chart. Do not accept predictions presented as facts (“A will break; B will reverse”) as complete answers.

### Teach four things to observe before the zone

Reveal the following one at a time. Do not put all four labels on the chart at once.

**On screen:** 

> Four observations worth making

**1. Direction and swing sequence**

> Is price making progressively higher or lower turns, or has it been moving sideways? Describe the recent structure before you interpret it.

**2. Overlap and pauses**

> Is price moving relatively directly, or spending more time moving back and forth? Overlap is an observation, not a standalone trading signal.

**3. Nearby structure**

> Is there another meaningful area nearby? The room between price and the next opposing area may matter if we later consider a scenario.

**4. Wider context**

> Does the local move sit inside a broader trend or trading range? A wider chart can add context, but it does not automatically overrule the local evidence.

### Ask what still remains unknown

**On screen:** 

> Before we reveal what happens next, name one thing the chart tells you and one thing it does not tell you yet.

**Feedback:**

> That distinction is useful. A good chart reader can describe what is visible and leave the rest open until there is more evidence.

### First instructor-chart micro-case

**Asset requirements:** One of your actual historical charts, cropped to show enough context to understand the current structure and the approach to a relevant zone. The initial image must be captured at a point before the zone interaction. Hide your markings, future candles, entry/exit labels, stop, target, P&L and final outcome. Record instrument, timeframe, date/time of the screenshot and what was knowable at that moment in the private asset register.

**Show initial state:** Plain chart only. If the zone itself is not obvious without your mark, do not draw it in advance; students should make a first reading.

**On screen:** 

> This time, the chart comes from my own trading. I am going to show you only the information available at this point—not what happened afterward.
>
> You do not need to agree with my eventual analysis. First, make your own observation.

**Prompt:**

> How is price approaching the area you think matters? Name one piece of evidence and one uncertainty.

**Response requirement:** One sentence for the observed evidence; one sentence for the uncertainty.

**Only after the response, reveal your markings.**

> “I marked this area because [describe the visible structure or prior reaction]. Before price reached it, I noticed [describe the approach without predicting the outcome]. One thing I did not know yet was [state a genuine uncertainty]. I was not treating the zone as a guarantee.”

Do not fill these blanks with invented rationale. They must be based on the actual trade and chart at that moment.

**After the reveal, show this note:**

> Your drawing may differ from mine and still be defensible. Compare the evidence and the boundaries, not just the shape of the mark.

**Hard stop:** End the micro-case before the entry decision or outcome. Do not click forward to the later candles. Say:

> We will study complete trade decisions later. For now, we are practising one part of that process: reading the approach without pretending we already know the result.

### Independent practice

**Controlled practice chart:** A third, unseen approach to a zone. Keep the eventual reaction hidden.

**Question 1:** Which description best fits the approach?
- Relatively directional with limited overlap.
- Overlapping and hesitant.
- Too little information to make a useful description.

**Question 2 — free response:** What contextual detail would you check next, and what remains uncertain?

**Scoring:**
- 1 point: accurate observation.
- 1 point: identifies relevant context or another area.
- 1 point: states a real uncertainty rather than treating the outcome as guaranteed.

**Feedback if the learner makes a firm prediction:**

> That is one possible scenario, but the candles shown do not establish it as fact. What can you point to on the chart, and what would you still need to observe?

### Takeaway and close

**On screen:** 

> **Read the route, not just the destination.** The approach to a zone adds context, but it does not determine what happens next.

**Short reflection:**

> Next time you look at a chart, describe the last few swings and the path toward a zone before drawing a conclusion about the reaction.

**Bridge to Lesson 10:**

> We have looked at the path toward an area. Next, we will watch what happens when price actually reaches it—and learn why one wick or candle is rarely enough to settle the question.

lessons.title: Rejection versus acceptance
lessons.summary: Distinguish a reaction away, sustained movement beyond, and inconclusive evidence.
lessons.content:
**In this lesson**

Distinguish a reaction away, sustained movement beyond, and inconclusive evidence.

### Open with the question

**On screen:** 

> Rejection or acceptance?

**On screen:** 

> Price has reached an area we care about. What happens next matters—but one candle rarely tells the whole story.
>
> We will read the evidence as it arrives, rather than looking at the finished chart and pretending the answer was obvious.

### Sequence A, first candle only

**On screen:** 

> What can we say from this candle alone?

Options:
- The candle guarantees rejection.
- It shows price traded through part of the area and then closed back away from the extreme.
- It proves price has accepted beyond the zone.
- There is not enough information to know what happens next.

Allow two choices: the factual observation and “not enough information about the next move” are both valid. Avoid grading this as a single-word pattern test.

**Feedback:**

> We can describe the candle's range and close. We cannot yet know whether later price action will reinforce this as rejection, establish activity beyond the zone, or remain mixed.

### Reveal the close and annotate the candle

**Reveal:** Add small arrows for the high/low excursion and closing location. Do not add a large red/green label saying “rejection.”

**Student-facing explanation:**

> A wick tells us price traded at those prices during the candle. The close tells us where the candle finished. Both are useful observations, but neither tells the entire story by itself.
>
> A move beyond the zone followed by a close back inside can be evidence consistent with rejection. We still need to see what price does afterward.

### Reveal follow-through: Sequence A

**Reveal:** Add the next two or three candles. In this sequence, price moves away from the zone and does not immediately reclaim the area.

**Prompt:**

> With these candles added, how would you describe the evidence now?

Options:
- Evidence consistent with rejection has strengthened.
- Price has clearly established itself beyond the zone.
- The evidence remains entirely unchanged.
- I need to inspect the sequence again.

**Model response:** “The close back away from the area followed by movement away strengthens the interpretation that this interaction was a rejection. It still does not guarantee that the zone will hold on another visit.”

**Feedback:**

> Your interpretation can become better supported without becoming certain. We are describing the sequence we can see—not promising the next one.

### Sequence B: close beyond the band, then continued action

**Chart B brief:** Similar visual layout but a different outcome. Price crosses the band and closes beyond it. Reveal only that candle first, then ask the learner to respond. After the initial response, reveal two additional candles that continue to spend time or close beyond the zone.

**Prompt after first candle:**

> Price has closed beyond the zone. Is that enough on its own to say the area has been accepted?

**Model response:** The close is relevant evidence that price finished beyond the zone, but one candle does not settle the classification.

**Reveal follow-through. Then prompt:**

> What changed after the next candles appeared?

**Model response:** Continued action beyond the zone makes acceptance a more reasonable current description than it was after the first candle alone. This remains a contextual judgement; price could still return through the zone.

**Student-facing copy:**

> **Acceptance is not a magic candle.** We are looking for evidence that price is spending time or continuing to act beyond an area, rather than just passing through it briefly.

### Sequence C: conflicting evidence

**Chart C brief:** Price crosses the area, closes beyond it, then returns to the band and moves back and forth. The excerpt should remain genuinely ambiguous rather than resolve cleanly in either direction.

**Prompt:**

> Does this sequence give you a clear answer, or is the evidence mixed?

Expected answer: Mixed/inconclusive. The price has moved beyond the area but has not shown clean, sustained behaviour on one side. More context or additional candles may be needed.

**Student-facing explanation:**

> “Inconclusive” is a valid chart-reading conclusion. It means the evidence shown does not justify a stronger claim yet. Good analysis is not a contest to produce a confident label for every chart.

### Three descriptions to keep separate

Reveal three definitions in turn:

**Rejection evidence:**
> Price tested or entered the area and then moved away in the visible sequence.

**Acceptance evidence:**
> Price showed continued or established activity beyond the area in the visible sequence.

**Inconclusive:**
> The available candles are mixed, too few or insufficient to distinguish the two descriptions.

**Copy beneath the definitions:**

> These terms describe the evidence so far. They do not guarantee what price will do next, and they are not trade signals by themselves.

### Practice: four short sequences

Show four short chart sequences in order. For every sequence, require a classification **and one sentence of evidence**. Let the learner revise after viewing the entire allotted sequence, but never show the final outcome before the classification step.

**Sequence 1:** Wick pierces the upper edge; candle closes back below; next candles move away.  
**Key:** Evidence consistent with rejection. Explain the close back away and subsequent movement. No guarantee of future resistance.

**Sequence 2:** Price closes beyond the zone; the next two candles also act beyond it.  
**Key:** Evidence consistent with acceptance beyond the zone. The relevant evidence is continued action, not just the first close.

**Sequence 3:** Price crosses, comes back, crosses again; sequence ends inside the band.  
**Key:** Inconclusive/mixed. A strong answer explicitly says why neither interpretation is settled.

**Sequence 4:** One large candle closes beyond the zone, but no later candles are shown.  
**Key:** A break and close have occurred in the excerpt; sustained acceptance is not established because follow-through is unavailable. “Too early to classify” is an excellent answer.

**Scoring per sequence (0–2):**
- 1 point for a defensible evidence category (inconclusive earns full credit where appropriate).
- 1 point for citing the right visible evidence and avoiding a guarantee.

**Feedback on overconfident answers:**

> Look at the candles you have, not the candles you wish you had. What is visible, and what information is still missing?

### Optional link to Lesson 9's micro-case

If the actual chart would make the answer ambiguous for reasons not taught yet, omit this repeat. The controlled exercises take precedence over forcing a personal chart into the lesson.

### Takeaway and bridge

**Takeaway:**

> **One candle is evidence, not a verdict.** Read the excursion, the close and what follows; stay willing to say “inconclusive.”

**Bridge:**

> Next, we will follow a zone across several visits. Instead of labelling it once and defending that label forever, we will practise updating our view as the evidence changes.
